description: We asked the AI models behind ChatGPT and DeepSeek where to buy jewellery in Singapore 139 times. Here's who they name, who they pick first, and why.
hubSummary: We asked the AI models behind ChatGPT and DeepSeek where to buy jewellery in Singapore 139 times. SK Jewellery was named in 97% of answers and never ranked first.
standfirst: We asked the AI models behind ChatGPT and DeepSeek where to buy jewellery in Singapore, 139 answers' worth. One brand showed up almost every time and was never the first pick. Here's who was, and what we'd do about it.
opening: Ask an AI assistant where to buy a wedding ring in Singapore and you'll get a confident, tidy list. We wanted to know who's on that list, so we asked. Not once: {{mention|n}} times, across the OpenAI and DeepSeek models, with the kinds of questions real shoppers type. First-time ring buyers. People saving in gold. Families planning a wedding set.

SK Jewellery was named in {{mention|pct0}} of those answers. If you ran marketing there, you'd probably take that number and go home happy. But being named and being chosen turn out to be very different things, and the gap between them is where the work is.
shortVersion: AI named POH HENG in every single answer, SK Jewellery in {{mention|pct0}} and Goldheart in {{brand0|pct0}}. TAKA made it into just {{brand8|pct0}}.
Poh Kong, Pandora, Swarovski and Clock Tower were never mentioned. Not once in {{mention|n}} answers.
SK was named in {{mention|pct0}} of answers, recommended in {{organicRecommendation|pct0}}, and ranked first in none of the 140 shortlists we collected.
For rings, AI's first pick was Love & Co. or JannPaul 98% of the time. For gold savers, it was BullionStar or UOB 80% of the time.
Adding an ethical-sourcing line to SK's description didn't move the shortlist: {{recommendationCurrentScore|pct0}} before, {{recommendationNewScore|pct0}} after.

sections.title: AI has a shortlist of Singapore jewellers, and it's short

blocks.text: We tracked nine jewellers. Three of them, POH HENG, SK Jewellery and Goldheart, are in almost every answer. TAKA is a coin flip. Tomei turned up twice.

blocks.title: Who AI names when you ask where to buy jewellery in Singapore
blocks.caption: Share of 139 AI answers that named each jeweller, without the question naming any brand.

blocks.text: Then there are the zeros. Poh Kong, Clock Tower, Pandora and Swarovski didn't appear in a single answer. These aren't obscure names. Pandora and Swarovski have stores in the same malls. But when a shopper asks an AI where to buy jewellery in Singapore, they simply aren't part of the conversation.
The two models mostly agreed, too. DeepSeek named SK every time; the OpenAI model did in {{openaiMention|pct0}} of its answers. This isn't one model's quirk.

sections.takeaway: Before you worry about what AI says about you, check whether it says your name at all. For four well-known brands here, the answer is no, and no amount of clever messaging fixes absence.

sections.title: Being named isn't the same as being picked

blocks.text: Here's where SK's good news gets complicated. Named in {{mention|pct0}} of answers. Actively recommended in {{organicRecommendation|pct0}}. And when we asked for a ranked top five, 140 shortlists in all, SK made the list about six times in ten and was never the first pick.

blocks.title: Named, recommended, ranked first: where SK Jewellery drops off
blocks.caption: SK Jewellery across 139 open answers and 140 ranked shortlists.

blocks.text: When SK does appear, it's usually near the bottom of the list, described as a sensible place to compare: mall stores, modern designs, 999 gold. All true, all pleasant, none of it a reason to go there first.

blocks.who: How the OpenAI model described SK in a ring buyer's shortlist

sections.takeaway: Track three numbers, not one: how often you're named, how often you're recommended, and how often you're first. Most brand dashboards stop at the first.

sections.title: AI sends ring buyers and gold savers somewhere else

blocks.text: So who gets the top spot? It depends entirely on what the shopper wants, and in each case AI has a clear favourite.

blocks.title: AI's first pick, by what the shopper wants
blocks.caption: Share of ranked shortlists where each brand came first. SK Jewellery came first in none.

blocks.text: For engagement rings it's Love & Co. or JannPaul, 49 times out of 50. Love & Co. is SK's own sister brand, so the group isn't losing that shopper, but SK Jewellery itself isn't in the running. JannPaul wins on something specific: the AI keeps praising its diamond education and cut-quality detail.

For people buying gold as savings, AI barely recommends jewellers at all. BullionStar and UOB take four of every five first picks, because the model thinks a saver wants live prices, tight spreads and buyback, and it says so. For wedding sets and Peranakan gold, POH HENG leads comfortably.

blocks.excerpt: Singapore-based bullion dealer with transparent live pricing, buyback options, and vault storage; well-suited to gold-as-savings buyers seeking physical bullion.
blocks.who: The OpenAI model on why BullionStar ranks first for gold savers

sections.takeaway: AI doesn't rank brands in general. It ranks them for a need. Find the two or three needs you should own, then look at exactly what AI praises the current winner for. That's your brief.

sections.title: AI knows what SK sells. It doesn't know why you'd choose it

blocks.text: We looked at what AI actually says when it mentions SK. The picture is consistent: contemporary designs, 999 pure gold, mall stores, good for gifting. Accurate, and completely generic.

blocks.title: The reasons to choose SK that AI almost never gives
blocks.caption: How often each selling point came up across the 135 answers that named SK Jewellery.

blocks.text: Now look at what it almost never says. Buyback came up in about one in ten mentions. Trade-in and upgrade value, 7%. Certified diamonds, once. Daily gold price, twice. Trusted family jeweller, never. These are the things shoppers in this category ask about before they hand over money, and AI doesn't connect any of them to SK.

sections.takeaway: Write down the five reasons someone should choose you. Then check whether AI ever gives those reasons. The gap between your list and AI's list is your content plan.

sections.title: We tried one fix. It barely moved anything, and that's useful

blocks.text: SK's website says its gemstones are ethically sourced. AI never mentions it. So we ran an experiment: take AI's own description of SK, add a short ethical-sourcing line, hand each version to the model as background, and ask for shortlists again.
All diamonds, gemstones, and gold used in our jewellery are sourced ethically and purchased from legitimate sources.
The shortlist didn't budge: SK made the top five {{recommendationCurrentScore|pct0}} of the time before and {{recommendationNewScore|pct0}} after. Still never first.

We also wanted to know how shoppers might take it. So we had the model role-play six kinds of jewellery buyer, from a first-time ring shopper to a retiree buying gifts, and react to each version in their own words. Then we scored how interested each reaction sounded, out of five. Overall interest went from {{buyerCurrentScore|fixed2}} to {{buyerNewScore|fixed2}}. A nudge, not a shift.

blocks.title: One added line, six kinds of buyer: who warmed up and who didn't
blocks.caption: How interested each role-played buyer sounded before and after the sourcing line was added.

blocks.text: The breakdown is more interesting than the average. The gold saver and the anniversary-upgrade buyer warmed up the most. The parent buying wedding gold cooled slightly. But read what they said and one thing jumps out: nobody talked about sourcing. They asked for today's gold price, workmanship charges, buyback terms, grading certificates.

blocks.excerpt: As someone buying mainly for savings, my next step would still depend on the day’s gold price, workmanship charges, and their buyback terms.
blocks.who: The gold-saver character, reacting to the new version

sections.takeaway: A values message on its own won't move you up an AI shortlist. Pair it with the specifics that buyer is already asking for, and test the pairing before you rewrite the website.

sections.title: Ask the same question two ways and you get two answers

blocks.text: One last thing, and it matters for anyone pasting an AI answer into a slide. We asked about engagement rings in several slightly different ways. With “places to consider”, SK appeared in two of five shortlists before our change and none after. With “rank the leading spots”, it went the other way: none before, two after.

blocks.title: Same shopper, different wording, different shortlist
blocks.caption: How many of five shortlists included SK Jewellery for each of the 14 shopping questions, before and after the added line.

rows.short: Ring buyer · rank the leading spots

blocks.text: Same shopper, same need, same brand. The wording of the question moved the result more than our message did. That's why we ask every question five times and ask it several ways. A single AI answer is an anecdote.

sections.takeaway: Never judge your AI visibility from one prompt. If an agency shows you a single screenshot, ask how many times they ran it.

recommendations.title: If I ran marketing at SK Jewellery
recommendations.intro: You already have the hard part: AI knows who you are. The job now is giving it reasons to put you first. Three things I'd do, in this order.

items.title: Own one need before you chase them all
items.body: Pick the shopper you most want, say the gold saver, and build the page AI is looking for: purity, today's price, workmanship charges and buyback terms, all in one place and kept current. Right now AI sends that shopper to a bullion dealer because the dealer answers those questions and you don't.

items.title: Turn your proof points into things AI can repeat
items.body: Buyback, trade-in, certified diamonds: if they're real strengths, write them down plainly, with specifics, where AI models can find them. “Trusted family jeweller” showing up zero times tells you the story you tell in-store isn't making it online.

items.title: Use sourcing as backup, not the headline
items.body: Ethical sourcing is worth saying. But our test suggests it reassures rather than persuades. Put it beside the certificate and the price, not instead of them, and test the pairing before you roll it out.

how.title: How we did this
paragraphs: We wrote 45 shopper questions about buying jewellery in Singapore and put each one to the OpenAI model that powers ChatGPT and to DeepSeek's model, through their APIs rather than the chat apps, five times each, on 19 September 2026. That's 450 answers. The {{mention|pct0}} figure comes from the {{mention|n}} answers to questions that didn't name any brand, so every mention is one the AI volunteered.
For the shortlist test, we gave the OpenAI model 14 shopping questions, five times each, with one of two descriptions of SK as background, and asked for a ranked top five each time: 140 shortlists.

For the buyer reactions, the same model played six shopper characters, five times per version. Those reactions are the model in character, not interviews with real customers. They are good for spotting what a message leaves unanswered, not for forecasting sales. We score them with a method published by independent researchers (arXiv:2510.08338).

SK Jewellery is a Singapore-based jewellery brand known for contemporary gold and diamond jewellery, with a strong presence in Singapore shopping malls and online retail.

### Overview
- **Origin:** Singapore  
- **Parent group:** SK Jewellery Group, which is associated with well-known brands such as **SK Jewellery**, **Soo Kee Jewellery**, and **Love & Co.**
- **Products:** Gold jewellery, diamond jewellery, engagement rings, wedding bands, fashion jewellery, and investment-grade gold items.
- **Market:** Primarily Singapore, with regional presence in parts of Southeast Asia.

### What SK Jewellery is known for
1. **999 Pure Gold**
   - SK Jewellery is especially known for its **999 pure gold** collections, which are popular for gifting, weddings, and wealth preservation.
   - Designs often include modern motifs, zodiac pieces, and cultural/festive collections.

2. **Diamond Jewellery**
   - The brand offers diamond rings, necklaces, earrings, and bracelets.
   - It has promoted diamond collections aimed at everyday luxury and bridal customers.

3. **Modern Retail Experience**
   - SK Jewellery positions itself as a more contemporary jeweller compared with traditional goldsmiths.
   - Stores are typically bright, modern, and mall-based.

4. **Bridal and Couple Jewellery**
   - Through the wider group’s brands, especially **Love & Co.**, the company has a strong focus on engagement rings and wedding bands.

### Typical customers
SK Jewellery appeals to:
- Shoppers buying gold for investment or gifting
- Couples looking for engagement or wedding jewellery
- Customers seeking modern gold and diamond designs
- Buyers interested in festive or culturally meaningful pieces, such as Chinese New Year or zodiac-themed jewellery

### Reputation
In Singapore, SK Jewellery is considered a mainstream and accessible jewellery retailer. It is not generally positioned as a high-luxury maison like Cartier or Tiffany & Co., but rather as a reputable regional jeweller offering a mix of traditional value items and modern designs.

### Where to buy
SK Jewellery products are sold through:
- Physical retail stores in Singapore
- The brand’s official website
- Selected e-commerce or marketplace channels, depending on region and availability
